column2: Return to the short straight steps. Each step took the current height and climbed by that height times the step's width. But climbing by a fraction of your own height is the same as multiplying your height. So a step one quarter wide multiplies by five quarters, whatever the height was. Four steps make five quarters to the fourth power, the endpoint we already drew.

Give one unit of time this fixed width, and split it into n cells. Now let the slope be x times the current height. Over that one unit of time, the fractional rate x gives each of n steps the multiplier one plus x over n. After all the steps, we have that multiplier raised to the n-th power. For a rate of one, this is the familiar compound-growth construction of e. More cells keep raising its endpoint, by less and less.

Now put those endpoints on the graph of our series. Change the rate, and the endpoint lands near the curve at that input, for rates above zero and below it. Near is still not a proof. Why should that limit be our series? Expand the finite product.

Each cell offers two choices. Keep its one, or take its x over n. Multiplying out the product means making those choices in every possible way. With four cells, that is sixteen ways, and they sort themselves by how many cells took x. For x squared, two cells must take it, and six pairs of cells can do that. So the coefficient of x squared is six times a quarter times a quarter, six sixteenths.

For any n and any k, count the same way. Pick cells one at a time. There are n options, then n minus one, then n minus two, until k cells are picked. Every set of k cells was counted k factorial times, so divide by k factorial. There is our factorial, earned a second way.

Now each picked cell brings its one over n, and those share out across the picks. So the coefficient of x to the k is one over k factorial, multiplied by a short chain of correction factors. The chain runs one, one minus one over n, one minus two over n, and so on. For our six sixteenths, that is one half, times one, times three quarters. Ask for more cells than exist, and one factor is exactly zero.

Hold k still, and let n grow. Here each bar shows how much of the series coefficient the product has reached. For any fixed k, every correction factor approaches one as n grows. The coefficient approaches exactly the coefficient in our series. The columns fill one at a time, but at every n, far columns are still nearly empty. If every column fills eventually, must the whole sum arrive?

Matching each fixed coefficient is not enough by itself, because there are also more and more terms. Here is a sum where that reasoning fails. Take n terms, each equal to one over n. Every fixed term shrinks to zero, so column by column the limit looks like zero. Yet the total is one, for every n. The weight slips out to columns further and further away.

Here is what makes our argument safe. Until k passes n, each correction factor lies between zero and one, and after that the chain is zero, so a whole chain never leaves that range. In absolute value, each finite-product term is no larger than the corresponding exponential-series term. These are the same ceilings we measured for the series, and n does not move them. Our warning sum has no such ceilings. Its column k can reach one over k, and those add up without limit.

Now measure the distance to E of x. It is at most the total of the gaps between each bar and its ceiling. Say we want that distance below one hundredth. Choose a cut before choosing n. Beyond the cut, every gap fits under the series tail, for every n at once.

We already know that series has a small tail, so push the cut out until the tail is small enough. Before the cut sit only finitely many columns, and each of their gaps closes. First make the shared tail small, then make the finitely many remaining coefficients close. That proves the whole expression converges.

Nothing in that argument asked x to be positive. Slide to minus three halves. The odd terms turn negative, so the bars alternate up and down. In absolute value they are the same bars under the same ceilings. So the same cut and the same number of cells bound the distance here too.

Push further, to minus three. One cell gives minus two. Two cells give one quarter, and three give exactly zero. Four cells give almost nothing, and then the values climb toward E of minus three. Decay needs a positive multiplier in every step, so the decay reading needs more than three cells. The algebra never asked for that. It never asked the values to climb steadily, and it never used a logarithm.

So for every real x, that n-th power approaches E of x. For bigger inputs, this argument asks for a later cut and more cells, but every input arrives. A rate of one gives the number e, one special case of this limit. A rate of x for one unit of time and a rate of one for x units of time make the same product. So the stepped drawing out to any input reaches the curve at that input. That pays the second debt.
